# How Urgent is it to Replace Worn Out CV Boots

A torn inner constant velocity (CV) boot on a Nissan Almera, or any front-wheel-drive vehicle, isn't just a cosmetic issue; it is an active failure mode that compromises the drivetrain's integrity. The image you provided shows a classic scenario: the rubber sleeve has split, exposing the internal splined shaft and grease to the elements. While you might be planning other maintenance like strut replacement, treating the CV boot requires immediate attention due to the physics of lubrication and wear rates.

### The Mechanics of Lubricant Loss

The inner CV joint is responsible for transmitting torque while allowing for suspension articulation. It operates on a principle similar to a bearing but with splines that engage under load. The rubber boot acts as a sealed containment vessel for high-viscosity grease. When this seal fails, two things happen simultaneously: the grease leaks out, and road contaminants rush in.

Grease is not an infinite resource. Once the volume drops below a critical threshold, the metal-to-metal contact between the splines increases friction dramatically. This generates localized heat that degrades the remaining lubricant instantly. Unlike the outer CV joint, which often fails catastrophically by ejecting the entire shaft, the inner joint typically suffers from gradual wear of the spline teeth or the needle bearings within the cage.

### The Timeline of Failure

You mentioned considering a six-month wait while addressing other issues like leaking struts. From an engineering standpoint, delaying boot replacement for that duration is high-risk. A torn boot does not have a "grace period." The rate of grease depletion is non-linear; once the seal is open, the flow is driven by centrifugal force during rotation and capillary action when the car is stationary.

Within weeks, you will likely see significant grease loss. If you wait six months, the probability of the joint seizing or the splines stripping approaches certainty. A stripped inner CV shaft often requires replacing the entire driveshaft assembly rather than just the boot, doubling the labor cost and downtime. In many cases, once the spline teeth are worn flat, the joint will grind to a halt under load, potentially locking the wheel if it occurs while driving at speed.

### Integrating with Other Maintenance Projects

Since you are already planning to replace the struts, this presents a unique opportunity for consolidated maintenance. The strut replacement process involves dropping the car or lowering it significantly to remove the wheels and lower control arms. This is the exact moment where CV joints are most accessible.

However, there is a trade-off in sequencing. If your current inner CV joint has been leaking grease onto the brake rotor or caliper for an extended period, you must inspect the braking components immediately after removing the boot. Brake fluid can mix with the leaked CV grease, altering its properties and potentially causing corrosion on the caliper piston seals or reducing friction efficiency. Similarly, if the grease has coated the wheel bearing hub, it could introduce contaminants that accelerate bearing wear.

### Implementation Strategy

When you go in to replace the struts, do not leave the CV boots behind. The labor hours required to remove the driveshafts and drop the suspension are already sunk costs for the job. Replacing the boot now is a preventative measure that avoids the much higher cost of a joint replacement later.

The procedure involves removing the old boot with care to avoid damaging the shaft seals, cleaning the splines thoroughly with brake cleaner or acetone, repacking the joint with high-quality synthetic grease (often lithium-complex based), and installing a new boot. The critical step is crimping the new boot securely using a dedicated hydraulic press tool. Hand-pressing the clamps can result in leaks that will ruin your work within days.

### Final Assessment

There is no valid technical reason to wait six months with a compromised inner CV boot. The failure mode is progressive and self-accelerating. By addressing it during your scheduled strut replacement, you mitigate the risk of driveshaft seizure, protect your braking system from contamination, and ensure that the drivetrain remains reliable for the life of the new suspension components.
